title: How to Restore Someone Who Has Fallen
subtitle: On Galatians 6 restoration, walking a fallen believer back to grace, and the difference between gentle restoration and church gossip

sections.title: When the News Reaches You
sections.body:
Sooner or later it will reach your desk. A leader in the affair. The deacon caught in the bottle again. The young couple living together. The respected woman who has been quietly cruel for years until it finally surfaced.

And before you do anything wise, watch your own heart, because it will move fast.

There is a dark satisfaction that visits a religious heart when someone falls, a quiet relief that it was not us, a sense of being confirmed as the good ones. Name it. It is the exact instinct that will poison the restoration before it begins. Paul saw it coming. When he told the Galatians to restore the one caught in sin, he added a warning in the same breath. Watch yourself, or you also may be tempted. The pastor who approaches a fallen brother feeling superior has already fallen further than the brother. The fall of another is not news to enjoy or repeat. It is a soul in danger, and the only question is whether anyone will go after it.

sections.title: The Goal Is Restoration, Not Removal
sections.body:
Churches are quick to remove and slow to restore, and we have the order backwards. The aim of confronting sin in a believer was never to purge the person. It was to recover him.

The word Paul uses meant to set a broken bone or mend a torn net. To make whole what is fractured.

Think about that picture. You do not set a bone by cutting off the limb. You do not mend a net by throwing it away. You handle the break with patience and skill until the thing can bear weight again. That is the church's calling toward the fallen, and it is a far harder calling than excommunication, which only takes a vote and a cold heart. Discipline that is not aimed at restoration is not Christian discipline. It is punishment wearing a Bible. There are times a person must be put out, and Paul commands that too, but even then the goal is the saving of the soul, not the protecting of our comfort. We are field hospitals before we are courtrooms. We exist to make broken people whole, including the ones who broke badly.

sections.title: Restore Gently, Which Is Not the Same as Softly
sections.body:
Paul gives one adverb for how to do this. Gently. Restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness.

Gentleness is not the absence of truth. It is strength that has chosen not to crush.

Do not confuse it with avoiding the hard word. Real restoration names the sin plainly, refuses the fog of excuses, and calls the fallen to genuine repentance, not a managed apology. But it does all of this without contempt, without enjoying the other's shame, without a single ounce of the harshness we so easily mistake for holiness. The goal is a person who comes home, not a person who is beaten into hiding. So speak the truth and keep your voice low. Confront and keep your hand open. Remember your own capacity for exactly this, or something worse, on a day when no one was watching you. The fallen believer is watching to learn whether the church is safe enough to be honest in. Your gentleness is the evidence. Your harshness is the door slammed shut.

sections.title: The Two Ditches: Gossip and Cover-Up
sections.body:
There are two ways to ruin a restoration, and most churches fall into one or the other. The first is gossip, dressed up as a prayer request, the news passed quietly until everyone knows and the fallen one has been tried in a hundred conversations he was never part of.

What we call a prayer request is, half the time, gossip with a hymn over it.

The other ditch is the cover-up, the instinct to bury serious sin to protect a reputation or a budget, which is how predators thrive and victims get silenced. Wisdom walks between them. Keep the circle as small as the situation allows and no smaller. Bring in only those who must restore, protect, or be warned. Tell the truth where the truth must be told, especially where someone was harmed, and refuse to tell it where it would only entertain. The rule is simple to say and hard to keep. Speak to the person, not about them. Involve those who can help, not those who will spread it. If you would not say it to his face, you have no business saying it behind his back.

sections.title: Restoration Is a Long Road, and You Walk It
sections.body:
Restoration is not a meeting. It is a road, often a long one, and the church that wants it over by next Sunday does not want restoration at all. It wants the embarrassment gone.

A bone takes weeks to set. A soul takes longer.

The fallen believer needs more than a confrontation and a probation. He needs someone to walk with him through the rebuilding, to believe a future for him when he cannot believe it himself, to hold the standard and hold his hand at the same time. That someone is costly to be. It is far easier to discipline a man and forget him than to disciple him back to life. But I think of where I would be if no one had stayed with me through my own worst stretch, and the answer is sobering enough to keep me at it. We are all one bad season from being the one who needs restoring. Treat the fallen the way you will pray to be treated on the day it is your name on the desk. Go after the one who fell. Stay until he can stand. That is the work, and it is holy.
